alt: Dog stretching its front legs naturally near its owner after getting up from rest
content:
Stretching in front of you is often a normal post-rest stretch, greeting ritual, or transition into activity. Repeated prayer-like posturing with illness or pain is different and needs veterinary attention.

Quick Answer

A normal stretch is usually brief and followed by ordinary movement. Some dogs also stretch during greetings or before play. What matters is whether the posture is voluntary, comfortable, and familiar.

Why Context Changes the Meaning

Watch what happens immediately afterward. A dog that rises, stretches once, then walks, eats, plays, and rests normally is very different from a dog repeatedly lowering the chest while keeping the rear elevated and appearing uncomfortable.

When Stretching Can Signal Discomfort

Repeated unusual stretching can accompany abdominal or musculoskeletal discomfort. Concern rises with vomiting, a tense or swollen abdomen, restlessness, appetite loss, weakness, or obvious pain.

What You Can Safely Observe

Do not force the limbs through a range of motion or press on a painful abdomen. Record a short video if the posture is intermittent and note whether it follows sleep, meals, exercise, or excitement.

When to Call the Veterinarian

Seek veterinary care for a new persistent pattern, stiffness, limping, reluctance to move, appetite change, vomiting, or pain. A distended abdomen, repeated unproductive retching, collapse, or severe distress requires urgent care.

content:
A bow when your dog sees you is commonly a play invitation or excited greeting. Body language and what happens next help distinguish a play bow from stretching or discomfort.

Quick Answer

A classic play bow has the front end lowered and the rear end up, often with loose movement, an open relaxed face, bouncing, or an invitation to chase. It is communication rather than a medical sign.

Stretching Can Look Similar

Some dogs also stretch when they approach a familiar person, especially after getting up. If the dog smoothly returns to normal movement and the posture is not repetitive or painful, this may simply be part of the greeting routine.

Read the Whole Body

Look at the whole sequence: loose wiggly movement and re-engagement support play; stiffness, reluctance to rise, repeated posturing, guarding the abdomen, or inability to settle points away from ordinary play.

How to Respond to the Bow

Respond to a friendly play bow with appropriate play if you want to engage. Avoid labeling every bow as dominance or submission; context is more useful than a single posture.

When a Bow-Like Posture Is Concerning

A new repetitive bow-like posture with vomiting, abdominal swelling, pain, weakness, or marked behavior change deserves veterinary assessment. Severe abdominal distress or collapse is urgent.

content:
Brief twitching or kicking during sleep is often associated with normal dreaming, but prolonged, violent, or unusual episodes—especially with abnormal behavior afterward—need closer evaluation.

Quick Answer

Small paw movements, facial twitches, eye movements, or brief vocal sounds can occur during normal sleep. The dog generally remains relaxed and wakes normally.

What to Record

Do not deliberately provoke an episode. If you are concerned, record video from a safe distance and note duration, breathing, body stiffness, drooling, urination, and how the dog behaves after waking.

Signs That Deserve Neurologic Assessment

Features that raise concern for seizure activity include sustained rigid or rhythmic whole-body movements, loss of normal awareness, heavy drooling, loss of bladder or bowel control, or a confused recovery period. No single sign should be diagnosed from an article alone.

Pain Can Also Disturb Sleep

Pain can also disturb sleep. A dog that repeatedly wakes, cries, changes position, avoids lying on one side, or struggles to rise may need assessment for discomfort rather than a neurologic disorder.

When It Is Urgent

Seek veterinary advice for a first suspicious seizure-like event or recurrent abnormal episodes. An episode lasting several minutes, repeated seizures without normal recovery, breathing difficulty, severe weakness, or collapse requires urgent veterinary care.

content:
Some dogs appear to sleep with partly open eyes during light or REM sleep, but persistent inability to close an eye, redness, discharge, cloudiness, or pain is not a normal sleep quirk.

Quick Answer

During light sleep, eyelids may not look fully closed and eye movement can sometimes be visible. The pale third eyelid may also cover part of the eye during sleep.

Check the Eyes While Awake

Check the eyes when the dog is fully awake. Both eyes should be compared for redness, squinting, discharge, cloudiness, swelling, unequal pupils, or an obvious inability to blink or close an eyelid normally.

When Eyelid Closure Is Abnormal

Facial nerve dysfunction, eyelid anatomy, eye pain, or surface disease can interfere with normal closure and tear-film protection. These possibilities require an eye examination rather than home treatment.

Avoid Unprescribed Eye Drops

Do not use human redness-relief drops or leftover eye medication. Eye problems can worsen quickly, and some medications are unsafe when the cornea is damaged.

When to See a Veterinarian

Arrange veterinary care for persistent incomplete closure while awake, squinting, rubbing, discharge, redness, cloudiness, or facial asymmetry. Sudden severe eye pain, trauma, or vision loss warrants prompt assessment.

content:
A tongue peeking out during relaxed sleep can be harmless, especially in some short-muzzled dogs or dogs with missing teeth. A new persistent change with breathing, swallowing, or neurologic signs needs attention.

Quick Answer

Deep relaxation can loosen the jaw enough for the tongue tip to protrude. Facial anatomy and missing teeth may make this more noticeable in some dogs.

What to Check After Waking

Check whether the tongue returns to a normal position when the dog wakes. Normal color, comfortable breathing, ordinary eating and drinking, and no mouth pain are reassuring contextual signs.

Mouth and Neurologic Clues

Dental disease, oral injury, swelling, jaw problems, or neurologic dysfunction can also alter tongue position. New drooling, dropping food, pawing at the mouth, facial asymmetry, or difficulty swallowing deserves examination.

What Not to Do

Do not pull on the tongue or place objects in the mouth of a distressed dog. If you can safely look without forcing the mouth open, note obvious swelling, bleeding, or a foreign object and contact a veterinarian for guidance.

Urgent Warning Signs

Breathing difficulty, blue or gray gums or tongue, collapse, severe facial swelling, or inability to swallow normally is urgent. Otherwise, discuss a new persistent tongue-position change with your veterinarian.

content:
Face rubbing after eating may be simple muzzle cleaning, but repeated vigorous rubbing can point to dental pain, food trapped in the mouth, or irritation of the skin, eyes, or ears.

Quick Answer

A brief wipe of the muzzle on a paw, rug, or furniture after eating can be normal grooming. Repetition, intensity, or signs of pain make the behavior more significant.

Clues From Eating and Chewing

Look for a connection to one type of food, chewing on one side, dropping food, bad breath, drooling, pawing at the mouth, or reluctance to eat hard items. These clues can point toward oral discomfort.

Other Sources of Facial Irritation

Skin irritation around the muzzle, an itchy ear, or an uncomfortable eye can also trigger face rubbing. Redness, swelling, discharge, squinting, hair loss, or a sudden one-sided pattern helps localize the problem.

Avoid Risky Mouth Checks

Do not probe deep in the mouth or try to remove an object that is embedded, sharp, or difficult to reach. Avoid human dental products and pain medicines.

When Face Rubbing Needs an Exam

Book an examination for persistent rubbing, oral pain, foul breath with discomfort, swelling, bleeding, eye signs, or reduced appetite. Facial swelling with breathing difficulty or severe eye pain requires prompt care.

Pawing repeatedly at the face often means something is uncomfortable around the eye, ear, mouth, or skin. The side involved and accompanying signs help determine urgency.

Quick Answer

Eye irritation can cause sudden pawing, squinting, tearing, redness, or light sensitivity. Corneal injury and foreign material can become painful quickly, so persistent eye signs deserve prompt attention.

Ear Discomfort

Ear pain may produce scratching near the face along with head shaking, odor, redness, or discharge. Do not insert cotton swabs or unprescribed drops into a painful ear.

Dental or Mouth Pain

Dental pain, a broken tooth, oral injury, or material caught in the mouth may cause pawing, drooling, bad breath, difficulty chewing, or dropping food. Avoid forcing open the mouth of a painful dog.

Skin Allergy and Swelling

Skin allergy, insect stings, or local irritation can affect the lips and face. Rapid facial swelling is more urgent, particularly if breathing or swallowing changes.

Protect the Face and Know the Red Flags

Use an e-collar if advised and necessary to prevent self-injury while arranging care. Seek prompt veterinary assessment for persistent eye pain, significant swelling, mouth injury, or severe discomfort; breathing difficulty is an emergency.

content:
Gagging immediately after gulping water can follow very fast drinking or brief throat irritation, but recurrent episodes may reflect swallowing or airway problems that need veterinary assessment.

Quick Answer

First determine whether the event is truly gagging, coughing, retching, or regurgitation. A short video can be extremely useful because owners and clinicians may use these words differently.

Fast Drinking

A dog that drinks extremely fast may cough or gag briefly after swallowing. Slow, supervised access may help some dogs, but do not restrict needed water simply to prevent an episode.

When Swallowing Needs Evaluation

Repeated difficulty swallowing, coughing with food or water, nasal discharge after drinking, regurgitation, or weight loss raises concern for problems involving the mouth, throat, esophagus, or airway.

Do Not Restrict Water Without Guidance

Do not force water into the mouth and do not use thickening agents or feeding modifications without veterinary direction. If aspiration is a concern, the safest plan depends on the underlying cause.

When Gagging After Water Is Urgent

Arrange veterinary evaluation when gagging repeatedly follows drinking or occurs with coughing, regurgitation, appetite change, feverish behavior, or weight loss. Breathing difficulty, blue or gray gums, collapse, or severe choking distress is urgent.

Some dogs simply like to rest with the head raised, but a new insistence on an elevated sleeping position can matter when it appears with coughing, noisy breathing, pain, or reduced exercise tolerance.

Quick Answer

A familiar preference for a pillow, armrest, or bed edge can be completely ordinary when the dog breathes comfortably and otherwise behaves normally.

A New Sleeping Position Matters More

A change in sleeping posture matters more than the posture by itself. Note whether the dog repeatedly abandons flat positions, seems restless, coughs at night, breathes faster or harder, or cannot settle.

Breathing and Airway Clues

Nasal congestion or upper-airway discomfort can make some positions less comfortable. Heart, lung, or airway disease can also affect breathing at rest, but sleeping position alone cannot identify the cause.

Pain Can Change Sleep Posture

Neck, back, or other musculoskeletal pain may lead a dog to choose a supported posture. Look for stiffness, reluctance to turn the head, difficulty rising, or sensitivity to movement.

When to Seek Care

Seek veterinary advice for a new persistent posture accompanied by cough, exercise intolerance, pain, or altered breathing. Labored breathing, blue or gray gums, collapse, or inability to rest comfortably requires urgent care.

content:
Dogs may wake panting because they are warm, excited from a dream, anxious, painful, or affected by a medical problem. Repeated unexplained nighttime panting deserves attention.

Quick Answer

A warm room, heavy bedding, or brief arousal from sleep can produce short-lived panting that settles once the dog is comfortable. Repeated episodes without an obvious heat or activity trigger deserve a closer look.

Pain at Night

Pain is an important possibility, particularly in older dogs. Restlessness, repeated position changes, stiffness, reluctance to jump, trembling, or difficulty rising can accompany discomfort.

Stress and Anxiety

Stress or anxiety may cause panting along with pacing, vigilance, trembling, or inability to settle. Identify environmental triggers such as storms, noises, visitors, or changes in routine before assuming the cause is behavioral.

Medication and Medical Clues

Some medications and medical conditions can increase panting. Record medication changes, thirst and urination, appetite, weight, coughing, abdominal appearance, and daytime energy for your veterinarian.

What to Monitor and When It Is Urgent

Count resting breaths when the dog is fully asleep and not panting if your veterinarian asks you to monitor respiration. Seek urgent care for labored breathing, blue or gray gums, collapse, severe weakness, a swollen abdomen, or rapidly worsening distress.
